Drones for crime prevention

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The City of Cape Town is using High Tech Crime surveillance to fight crime in Cape Town

Summary:
The City of Cape Town is planning to use Remotely Piloted Aircraft –RPAs, more commonly known as drones - in drug busts, land invasions, fire mapping, Search and Rescue, Agricultural mapping and many other applications. To date they have been used during drug busts in Mitchell’s Plain at night and the Police have been able to monitor and track people escaping and hiding from officials. They are being flown over the Standfontein area, a notorious part of Cape Town where cable thieves burn the plastic off copper cable under the cover of darkness before they take it to scrap dealers. There are numerous uses for drones but currently the City has to apply for special permission from the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) to use them.


Further information:
For the past year, the CAA has been drafting legislation that will control the use of RPAs because they believe they pose a risk to aircraft and people. Yet when you talk to the official RPA bodies like the SA Radio Controlled Aerial Operators they say there is no data that substantiates these claims and that there hasn’t been one accident in the last two years. SARCAO is the largest body of enthusiasts and professionals in Africa, and they have offered all the data they have collected. They have even drafted regulations and safety guidelines for the CAA and to date have not had any response from them
The CAA says they are trying to control the hobbyists but the kind of planes hobbyists are flying are so small they can’t harm you, if they do make contact with you their blades break off. There are about 20 commercial operators who use bigger craft for film shoots, rhino poaching etc and they are all highly skilled and value their equipment. All these craft are flown by an operator and a spotter.
One of the arguments the CAA has put forward is that they could fly into commercial aircraft, but SARCAO says people who own expensive RPA’s are highly unlikely to go and fly them anywhere near an airport because most airports are surrounded by quite dangerous public spaces, inhabited by criminals.
The CAA say they will have the legislation drafted by the end of March and they are proposing that everyone get tested for radio competency, flying competency and a number of other areas, yet the very people they are wanting to licence are more qualified to operate the RPAs than the CAA. In effect, the CAA is wanting people to be qualified pilots to fly what is essentially a toy. SARCAO are wanting to know on what data the CAA is basing this whole legislative process and whether or not the CAA has the finances to set up an entire department to test and licence possibly 20 people?
Radio controlled planes have been operating in SA for the decades without any legislation. Some of those aircraft are nearly as big as real planes with 8 meter wing spans, and yet they are not being legislated.
The people using Commercial and industrial RPA’s are not flying in commercial airspace, they also do not fly high enough and they can only fly for about 15 minutes. SARCAO say the CAA have had far more accidents under their watch in the last two years with 20 deaths in real aircraft, yet under SARCAO’s watch, there have has not been a single injury, let alone any deaths.
We will have access to the largest collection of footage from SARCAO who have flown in just about every situation.

Viewing Notes:
21/04/2015 04:26:11 PM
Amalia, WYNAND, DUNCAN – George to view later on We transfer

• Intro is boring “the city of cape town is testing...” we need a more dramatic first couple of sentences... we are on the streets a block away from a drug bust out with the cops and criminals are making a run for it nearby – something like that? please write it...
• Hennie’s intro visuals are really not great. we see him blankly staring on a screen for a long time then John blankly staring at him for a long time, please change, show their logo, add in other visuals
• Vince can FTP you more drone visuals – Please let Wynand know / Wynand will talk to Vince
• Where you do use the drone visuals over the train/landscapes you don’t indicate that these are drone visuals.
• At the very end John comes back and says that shows how great drones are... there is nothing that shows the efficacy of the drone - we don’t see them moving in or arresting anyone / recovering drugs? Not clear at all.
• It’s not clear that out on the streets you are with two drone operators and separate scenes... seems like they are all one scene...
• Also does it film infra – red how would they find people at night?
• Please add in more dramatic visuals at the end.
• Please come in at 10

DUNCAN
• Nothing that he is very worried about legally.
• Double check that we can’t see faces of any of the suspects – you indicated that there was a place where there could have been someone we were seeing who we should not be seeing
• Doesn’t understand how Cape Town is officially using them but they are then illegal? How are they doing this? Liz please explain that they get special permission for each flying event and that this is an interim situation.

George please send your notes soon as you can
Thanks!
Amalia

Press Release:


Crime-fighting drones
Remote controlled drones are all the rage. In Alaska, drones are used to count sea lions and in the USA they monitor drug trafficking across borders. Now the City of Cape Town wants to get in on the act and use drones for drug busts, search and rescue operations and agricultural mapping. But the Civil Aviation Authority isn’t giving the project lift off. Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


Script: We are heading into gang land on the Cape Flats, about to go in on a drug bust with the special policing unit. We are few streets away from the suspect’s house, they sent up a drone with a thermal camera in advance of the raid so they can see if anybody’s fleeing, or throwing weapons or drugs over walls.
Link “There is a drone currently in the air at the moment its about 82 meters above us its very difficult to see, almost impossible in fact and its picking up figures running around the streets and on occasions dodging into buildings
Script: Hennie Louw, a private contractor, with a background in policing, is one of two service providers demonstrating their drones for the City of Cape Town tonight.
Hennie “So basically you are flying it to get the diamond back so you flying flying and there comes the diamonds so now you know if that diamond is in the middle it is flying back to you
John “ I see “
Hennie “So he knows the orientation of the drone that’s all of us standing there now we know our battery life we have got our satellite up there so we always know on our flight screen what is happening on the drones
John “This is the pilot over here and if you think that he looks young that is because he is and there is very good reason for that he has gaming experience
LINK “We are now making our way to a house down the road from where the drone was deployed because apparently there has been one arrest. We understand that a stash of heroin has been found”
Script: JP Smith the City of Cape Town’s Mayoral Committee member for Safety and Security has been testing drones in various applications within the City,
JP” Not a big haul but a haul we would not have got if we didn’t know where to look, there are a few refinements A we have to rehearse this a lot it is going to take a lot of rehearsing and practice and B we have to designate our members so we can see clearly who’s who
Script: Most people call them drones, but that has negative connotations because of their use in war zones, so instead, they are called remotely piloted aircraft, RPAs.
Link “There is really no end to how RPAS can be used from helping to curb Rhino poaching to being deployed in the fight against crime and even delivering medicine who knows in the future their might be 100s of them flying overhead but there is a concern that strict new regulations introduced by the CAA authority could stifle this brand new sector “
Script: Hennie Kieser president of the Commercial Unmanned Aircraft Association of South Africa, CUASSA, and has been part of stakeholder meetings with the CAA.
Hennie Kieser “If you just go through the 101 legislation to see how many documents and manuals and procedures and organograms you have to generate and going to the air servicing licencing council the time from when you start to when we estimate the fastest you will get a licence is 3 to 6 months minimum and the cost will be R50000 on the administration side so you can get permission to fly an RPAs of R3000 doing photography for a real estate agent and that doesn’t make economical sense
Script: FC Hamman and his son Tim are highly regarded in the feature film industry as some of the country’s top drone camera operators. In June 2013 FC was arrested and his drone confiscated while filming outside the hospital where the late Nelson Mandela was being treated.
FC Hamman “We were recording some footage for Carte Blanche on the day in my opinion we were operating within the rules that we understood at the time not flying higher than 150 feet and not flying over people and over roads. They didn’t tell us what we were arrested for “
Script: The charges were eventually dropped
Script: For the last year the Civil Aviation Authority has banned the use of drones while it drafts legislation to regulate them, it’s been a massive blow to this burgeoning industry
Hennie Kieser “ The vast majority of people including my own company does not even operate in SA that’s why I am currently in Rio marketing my products and my skills even setting up manufacturing facilities outside SA which obviously isn’t to the benefit to our own country but how can you not do it if you are not allowed to operate in your own country “
FC Hamman “ I think it is a very grey area at the moment because we are operating under radio controlled rules and my understanding of that is we are allowed to fly below 150 ft line of sight …although civil aviation said there was a ban I don’t understand which law controls that”
Script: But Subash Devkaran of the South African Civil Aviation Authority says currently the use of all RPAS is illegal
Subash “Given that there is no controlled environment or regulatory framework currently which is very specific to RPAs one may find that the public or members of certain sectors of the public utilises technology in a very unsafe manner
Hennie Kieser “We have been doing it safely for the last 5 to 10 years and we can continue to do that but there is a massive lack of understanding….. We know that normal aviation you have to be extremely strict because there are people physically in those aircraft on a 5kg RPAS there is no people in the aircraft and the risk when something should go wrong is negligible but the benefits is massive
Script: The City has to apply for special permission to fly drones while they wait for the regulations to be finalised.
Link: So onto or second location for the night which are those flats in the background and we understand they have been taken over by a gang. The drone will be sent up into the sky in a few minutes and communicate with the personnel on the ground and a raid will be carried out
Script: It’s the second service provider’s turn to show off his drone tonight.
Upsound “Is the wind grabbing you, it’s the wind , I need a car on that . We need a car on that thing
JP “Are you loosing signal or connection with it”
Ja do you have a torch
No its too far
Does it have a fail safe to come home?
Link “Well it seems we have experienced a few teething problems on the second operation the drone initially deployed properly over the flats in the background and then through a combination of wind and other technical issues has disappeared over the horizon
Script: All drones are supposed to have what is called a failsafe device which means when you lose control for whatever reason, the drone automatically returns and lands at the same place from which it’s launched. Failures like this, although rare, are exactly what the Civil Aviation Authority and the drone operators are most concerned about.
Link “ It is clear RPAS are effective in the fight against crime but there are inherent risks but that is something the operators say they are conscious of and that steps can be taken to limit those dangers without having to resort to stringent legislation
John “ The City of Cape Town for example is very keen to use these drones in the fight against crime but under the new regulations will that be difficult? “
Subash “If it’s for example for railway security or for cable theft operations in remote areas, I think it probably would not be however if one is intending to fly an RPA over the City of CT over the streets of Cape Town that would certainly be a very high risk operation and this technology although its applications are tremendous at this stage its safety has not yet been proven
Hennie Kieser “They will rather see 10 people die in a gang war than put 5kg RPAS over that whole situation and save those 10 people with the risk of maybe one day 1 in a million have an RPAS fall on someone and in the worst case you will have a few cuts
Script: Normally the CCA would apply the international regulations on drones but these will only be ready in 2028, so they are pushing ahead locally. They promised they would have them out by the end of March. Currently they are waiting for a response from the Minister of Transport.
Hennie Kieser “In August they invited industry to a workshop which was the rule making workshop and then them themselves said we are going to put on new hats because we can’t do it identical to current aviation but when we entered into the workshop everything was a mirror of civil aviation which is ridiculous they are over regulating to such an extent that there is no ways they can even try to regulate it
Script: The greatest concern is the danger posed by the amateur operators, illustrated recently when a drone cut short a display by the Air Force’s Silver Flacons. Commercial operators all agree that there is a need for safety standards and licencing of craft
John “How would you respond to the concern to members of the flying public who are very worried about a drone flying into a plane’s flight path?
FC Hamman “We are not supposed to operate closer than 5 nautical miles from any commercial airport so by the time a plane goes past us its way way above the height that we are allowed to fly so we are only allowed to fly up to 150ft and full size aircraft are not allowed to fly near that height even helicopters can’t fly that high without permission so I think there is a very safe space in between real airspace and where we operate
Hennie Kieser “Worldwide this is the fastest growing industry the biggest opportunities for job creation and for making a difference in everybody’s country. So it is just a matter of time and I hope that our politicians will soon realise that they need this technology off the ground as soon as possible but with the least red tape as possible
Script: It’s the 3rd bust of the evening, fortunately we still have the first drone, and it’s up in the air quickly. Tensions are running high.
UPSOUND banging door
Script: The sting is on a notorious drug den. It’s happening very fast, the suspects are escaping over the roof.
UPSOUND “Skit hom” “Waar is die drone”
Link “Well that really did show the value of the drones a rapid deployment and an absolute synergy between the drone and the people on the ground
John “So JP the end of a long night what have you learnt
JP “Our guys have developed their strategies over a long time they have got a very specific MO and you will have to train them to take full advantage of the eye in the sky Secondly There is definitely a tactical advantage to the drone we always lose 1/3 or ¼ of the people at the premises and that gives you the advantage of seeing where they are running and fetching
John “So you obviously believe think this is worth pursuing
JP “It’s largely a non-emergency use in other words a passive use where you are going to mop up a disaster scene afterwards or you are checking fire breaks or you are checking cracks in bridges engineering purposes waterways solid waste issues anti land invasion to check for urban creep subject of course to us being able to navigate the CAA recs”
Script: Industry says drones are on the cutting edge of technology, have a myriad of applications at a fraction of the cost of normal aircraft. They will continue to fight with the authorities until reasonable regulations are in place.

Upsound “Is the wind grabbing you, it’s the wind , I need a car on that . We need a car on that thing JP “Are you loosing signal or connection with it” Ja do you have a torch No its too far Does it have a fail safe to come home? Link “Well it seems we have experienced a few teething problems on the second operation the drone initially deployed properly over the flats in the background and then through a combination of wind and other technical issues has disappeared over the horizon Script: All drones are supposed to have what is called a failsafe device which means when you lose control for whatever reason, the drone automatically returns and lands at the same place from which it’s launched. Failures like this, although rare, are exactly what the Civil Aviation Authority and the drone operators are most concerned about. Link “ It is clear RPAS are effective in the fight against crime but there are inherent risks but that is something the operators say they are conscious of and that steps can be taken to limit those dangers without having to resort to stringent legislation John “ The City of Cape Town for example is very keen to use these drones in the fight against crime but under the new regulations will that be difficult? “ Subash “If it’s for example for railway security or for cable theft operations in remote areas, I think it probably would not be however if one is intending to fly an RPA over the City of CT over the streets of Cape Town that would certainly be a very high risk operation and this technology although its applications are tremendous at this stage its safety has not yet been proven Hennie Kieser “They will rather see 10 people die in a gang war than put 5kg RPAS over that whole situation and save those 10 people with the risk of maybe one day 1 in a million have an RPAS fall on someone and in the worst case you will have a few cuts Script: Normally the CCA would apply the international regulations on drones but these will only be ready in 2028, so they are pushing ahead locally. They promised they would have them out by the end of March. Currently they are waiting for a response from the Minister of Transport. Hennie Kieser “In August they invited industry to a workshop which was the rule making workshop and then them themselves said we are going to put on new hats because we can’t do it identical to current aviation but when we entered into the workshop everything was a mirror of civil aviation which is ridiculous they are over regulating to such an extent that there is no ways they can even try to regulate it Script: The greatest concern is the danger posed by the amateur operators, illustrated recently when a drone cut short a display by the Air Force’s Silver Flacons. Commercial operators all agree that there is a need for safety standards and licencing of craft John “How would you respond to the concern to members of the flying public who are very worried about a drone flying into a plane’s flight path? FC Hamman “We are not supposed to operate closer than 5 nautical miles from any commercial airport so by the time a plane goes past us its way way above the height that we are allowed to fly so we are only allowed to fly up to 150ft and full size aircraft are not allowed to fly near that height even helicopters can’t fly that high without permission so I think there is a very safe space in between real airspace and where we operate Hennie Kieser “Worldwide this is the fastest growing industry the biggest opportunities for job creation and for making a difference in everybody’s country. So it is just a matter of time and I hope that our politicians will soon realise that they need this technology off the ground as soon as possible but with the least red tape as possible Script: It’s the 3rd bust of the evening, fortunately we still have the first drone, and it’s up in the air quickly. Tensions are running high. UPSOUND banging door Script: The sting is on a notorious drug den. It’s happening very fast, the suspects are escaping over the roof. UPSOUND “Skit hom” “Waar is die drone” Link “Well that really did show the value of the drones a rapid deployment and an absolute synergy between the drone and the people on the ground John “So JP the end of a long night what have you learnt JP “Our guys have developed their strategies over a long time they have got a very specific MO and you will have to train them to take full advantage of the eye in the sky Secondly There is definitely a tactical advantage to the drone we always lose 1/3 or ¼ of the people at the premises and that gives you the advantage of seeing where they are running and fetching John “So you obviously believe think this is worth pursuing JP “It’s largely a non-emergency use in other words a passive use where you are going to mop up a disaster scene afterwards or you are checking fire breaks or you are checking cracks in bridges engineering purposes waterways solid waste issues anti land invasion to check for urban creep subject of course to us being able to navigate the CAA recs” Script: Industry says drones are on the cutting edge of technology, have a myriad of applications at a fraction of the cost of normal aircraft. They will continue to fight with the authorities until reasonable regulations are in place. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The City of Cape Town is using High Tech Crime surveillance to fight crime in Cape Town
metadata.Summary: The City of Cape Town is planning to use Remotely Piloted Aircraft –RPAs, more commonly known as drones - in drug busts, land invasions, fire mapping, Search and Rescue, Agricultural mapping and many other applications. To date they have been used during drug busts in Mitchell’s Plain at night and the Police have been able to monitor and track people escaping and hiding from officials. They are being flown over the Standfontein area, a notorious part of Cape Town where cable thieves burn the plastic off copper cable under the cover of darkness before they take it to scrap dealers. There are numerous uses for drones but currently the City has to apply for special permission from the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) to use them.
metadata.Further information: For the past year, the CAA has been drafting legislation that will control the use of RPAs because they believe they pose a risk to aircraft and people. Yet when you talk to the official RPA bodies like the SA Radio Controlled Aerial Operators they say there is no data that substantiates these claims and that there hasn’t been one accident in the last two years. SARCAO is the largest body of enthusiasts and professionals in Africa, and they have offered all the data they have collected. They have even drafted regulations and safety guidelines for the CAA and to date have not had any response from them The CAA says they are trying to control the hobbyists but the kind of planes hobbyists are flying are so small they can’t harm you, if they do make contact with you their blades break off. There are about 20 commercial operators who use bigger craft for film shoots, rhino poaching etc and they are all highly skilled and value their equipment. All these craft are flown by an operator and a spotter. One of the arguments the CAA has put forward is that they could fly into commercial aircraft, but SARCAO says people who own expensive RPA’s are highly unlikely to go and fly them anywhere near an airport because most airports are surrounded by quite dangerous public spaces, inhabited by criminals. The CAA say they will have the legislation drafted by the end of March and they are proposing that everyone get tested for radio competency, flying competency and a number of other areas, yet the very people they are wanting to licence are more qualified to operate the RPAs than the CAA. In effect, the CAA is wanting people to be qualified pilots to fly what is essentially a toy. SARCAO are wanting to know on what data the CAA is basing this whole legislative process and whether or not the CAA has the finances to set up an entire department to test and licence possibly 20 people? Radio controlled planes have been operating in SA for the decades without any legislation. Some of those aircraft are nearly as big as real planes with 8 meter wing spans, and yet they are not being legislated. The people using Commercial and industrial RPA’s are not flying in commercial airspace, they also do not fly high enough and they can only fly for about 15 minutes. SARCAO say the CAA have had far more accidents under their watch in the last two years with 20 deaths in real aircraft, yet under SARCAO’s watch, there have has not been a single injury, let alone any deaths. We will have access to the largest collection of footage from SARCAO who have flown in just about every situation.
